endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Data cleaning should be done to ensure data integrity while maintaining alignment with the intended model deployment data environment. Traditional methods of dealing with missing data or outliers don’t always work well against live, production data, and can impact performance.

A Practical Guide to Evaluating Artificial Intelligence Imaging Models in Scientific Literature
endorsements.quote: First, ensure the practice has the necessary infrastructure and resources to integrate the AI model, including compatibility with existing practice equipment.

endorsements.title: The EU AI Act: implications and compliance guidance for healthcare facilities
endorsements.quote: Site-specific testing to ensure the AI performs consistently on local hardware, checks to identify if the AI performs as expected in the local environment, and interoperability testing to ensure seamless data flow between the AI and existing EHR or PACS systems.

endorsements.quote: Validation would require confirmation that the locked model is compatible with local ECG acquisition, preprocessing, and data-transfer systems, followed by testing in a local or otherwise suitably representative population independent of model development.

endorsements.quote: Successful implementation requires verification of interoperability across the entire digital pathology ecosystem rather than validation of the AI algorithm alone [ 11].

evidence.title: Connecting Risk Prediction to Intervention: Evidence from a Randomized Trial Testing Patient Navigation and Education to Improve Postpartum Outcomes
evidence.venue: American journal of obstetrics & gynecology MFM
evidence.outcome: Compatibility of model input definitions with local medical record data during real-time risk scoring
evidence.effect: Coordinators reported time-intensive abstraction, discrepancies between variable definitions in administrative data (model development) and medical records (recruitment), and missing data.
evidence.quote: Coordinators reported challenges to risk calculator use, including time-intensive abstraction, discrepancies between variable definitions in administrative data (model development) and medical records (recruitment), and missing data.

evidence.title: Utilizing standardized nursing terminologies in implementing an AI-powered fall-prevention tool to improve patient outcomes: a multihospital study

evidence.effect: Only 4 of 6 concept-model constructs mapped to local data; KPCS data unavailable at site D; medication mapped to local drug classes; local statements covered 48.0%-86.7%.
evidence.quote: Four of the 6 constructs in the concept model were successfully mapped to local data elements.

evidence.title: In vivo clinical effectiveness of artificial intelligence screening for acute coronary syndrome: testing real-world performance
evidence.outcome: Differences between live input data and completed retrospective data
evidence.effect: Data differences affected about 13% of encounters, 96% from chief complaints; live vs completed-data model agreement 97.2%, Kappa 92.3%; sensitivity barely changed
evidence.quote: These data differences impacted about 13% of all encounters; 96% of all data differences were associated with the arrival chief complaints.

evidence.title: Evolution of an Artificial Intelligence-Powered Application for Mammography
evidence.outcome: Technical failures associated with local configuration and examination parameters
evidence.effect: Technical defects exceeded the 10% threshold, predominantly involving incomplete image analysis; identified contributors included mammography unit configuration problems and incorrect examination parameters.
evidence.quote: Key contributing factors included mammography unit configuration problems, incorrect examination parameters set by technicians, PACS technical issues, and AI developer errors.

evidence.title: Development and Implementation of a Machine Learning Model for Prediction of Surgical Case Duration
evidence.venue: Joint Commission journal on quality and patient safety
evidence.outcome: Effect of inconsistent software configuration and duration definitions on prediction error
evidence.effect: User-adjusted settings and inconsistent prep/wrap inclusion gave MAE 35.3 min, f30min 0.52, f10% 0.09; vendor-recommended Epic settings with standardized definitions gave MAE 20.1 min, f30min 0.81, f10% 0.37.
evidence.quote: Standardizing workflow elements-specifically, consistent inclusion of prep/wrap time and use of vendor-recommended Epic settings-substantially improved performance (MAE = 20.1 min, f<sub>30min</sub> = 0.81, and f<sub>10%</sub> = 0.37).

evidence.title: Technical Adequacy of Fully Automated Artificial Intelligence Body Composition Tools: Assessment in a Heterogeneous Sample of External CT Examinations
evidence.outcome: Failures from input specification mismatch (incorrect DICOM header voxel dimensions)
evidence.effect: Anisometry error accounted for 81 of 92 (88.0%) exams where all three tools failed; all three tools failed whenever it occurred.
evidence.quote: A single type of image processing error (anisometry error, due to incorrect DICOM header voxel dimension information) accounted for 81 of 92 (88.0%) examinations in which all three tools failed, and all three tools failed whenever this error occurred.

evidence.title: Large-Scale Evaluation and Liver Disease Risk Prediction in Finland's National Electronic Health Record System: Feasibility Study Using Real-World Data

evidence.effect: Using structured data only 33/51,275 identified as low risk and 308/51,275 (<1%) as moderate risk; with approximation and free text 18,895 (37%) low and 2125 (4%) moderate; no high-risk identified because waist-hip ratio was missing.
evidence.quote: We found that Kanta currently lacks many CLivD risk model input parameters in the structured format required to calculate precise risk scores.

evidence.title: Performance Degradation between Development and Deployment of a Predictive Model for Central Line-Associated Bloodstream Infections in Hospitalized Children
evidence.outcome: Compatibility of model input features between development data and real-time production data
evidence.effect: Train/serve skew and challenging feature translation between real-time and historical data models caused performance to fall from AUROC 0.97 to <0.60.
evidence.quote: Primary root causes included train/serve skew, feature leakage, and overfitting.

evidence.title: Deep learning for atrioventricular regurgitation diagnosis: an external validation study
evidence.outcome: Proportion of eligible echocardiograms for which the model could return a prediction
evidence.effect: Model returned predictions for 578 of 1541 eligible TTEs (38%); performance analysis limited to these cases, indicating mismatch between model input requirements and local acquisition practices.
evidence.quote: Among 1541 eligible TTEs, the model returned predictions for 578 studies (38%).
evidence.sample_unit: echocardiography studies with model predictions (of 1541 eligible)

evidence.title: Deploying machine learning models in clinical settings: a real-world feasibility analysis for a model identifying adult-onset type 1 diabetes initially classified as type 2
evidence.outcome: local input availability across HIE facilities
evidence.effect: Only 415/536 facilities shared diagnoses; among these, 87% shared medications, 87% vital signs, 68% labs, and 21% procedures.
evidence.quote: Out of 536 health facilities contributing to the HIE data pool, we found that only 415 share diagnoses records, which are crucial for identifying T2D patients and building cohorts for this study.
evidence.sample_unit: adult type 2 diabetes patients in regional HIE dataset (2,564,877 patient cross-sections)

evidence.title: Identifying eligible patients for the Australian national lung cancer screening program in primary care: A cross-sectional study using clinical decision support systems and evaluating PLCOm2012 data quality
evidence.outcome: Availability of PLCOm2012 input variables in general practice EMRs
evidence.effect: In 933 audited records, missing data were education 100%, ethnicity 58%, BMI 57%, daily cigarette consumption 33%; pack-years calculable for only 17.2% of 1,315 records.
evidence.quote: A subset of 933 records was assessed for PLCOm2012 variables, revealing substantial data gaps (% missing): education level (100 %), ethnicity (58 %), BMI (57 %), and daily cigarette consumption (33 %).

evidence.title: External Validation, Recalibration, and Extension of a Prediction Model of Early Acute Kidney Injury in Critically Ill Children Using Multicenter Data
evidence.effect: Original coefficients AUROC was 0.74 in PEDSNET-VPS versus 0.39 in PDC, where two of seven features were missing.
evidence.quote: The AUROC was 0.74 in the PEDSNET-VPS dataset and 0.39 in the PDC dataset, which is missing two of the seven features as previously described.

evidence.title: Testing Transferability of a Mortality Risk Model for Interhospital Transfer Using Real-World Electronic Health Records: External Validation and Model Enhancement
evidence.outcome: Availability of model input variables in local production EHR data
evidence.effect: Functional status measures were missing in 91.3% and comorbidity indicators in 96-99% of encounters; vitals and labs 42-43% missing, limiting the original feature set.
evidence.quote: Substantial missingness was observed across several SafeNET predictors: Vital signs and laboratory values showed 42–43% missingness, while functional status measures (91.3%) and comorbidity indicators (96–99%) were missing in the majority of cases.

evidence.title: Transporting a pediatric surgical site infection prediction model to the electronic health record: external validation, harmonization, and recalibration
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Compatibility of model predictor definitions with EHR data
evidence.effect: Diagnosis-code predictor misalignment between registry and EHR degraded performance; omitting open-ended diagnosis-code indicators improved c-statistic to 0.70, Brier 0.03, slope 0.81, O/E 1.35.
evidence.quote: After omitting open-ended diagnosis-code indicators, performance improved, with c-statistic 0.70, Brier score 0.03, calibration slope 0.81, and O/E ratio 1.35.

evidence.title: Deep learning for freezing of gait assessment using inertial measurement units: a multicentre validation study
evidence.outcome: false positives from missing IMU channels
evidence.effect: Pre-trained #FPs/trial were 4.787 Federal, 1.052 Twente, and 2.462 Xuanwu in one/two-IMU datasets.
evidence.quote: Similarly, Fig. 3 c, d, and f illustrate the model’s tendency to generate multiple FPs in datasets with only one or two IMUs, i.e., Federal, Twente, and Xuanwu, potentially due to zero-filling of missing channels to match the 5-IMU input of the pre-trained model.

commentary.bottom_line: Nineteen studies show that missing, mismatched, or misconfigured inputs degrade AI outputs in local systems, but no study tests whether verifying input compatibility before deployment prevents these errors. Seven sources endorse the practice based on expert judgment and the documented hazard.

perspectives.view: None of the 19 supplied studies tests whether pre-deployment verification of input compatibility reduces incorrect outputs. The hazard evidence includes one randomized trial and several prospective deployments, and these studies consistently report missing or mismatched inputs. They show that the problem exists but do not show that a verification step prevents it.

Train/serve skew reduced AUROC from 0.97 to below 0.60 in one report. In another, missing two of seven features dropped AUROC from 0.74 to 0.39. Incorrect DICOM voxel dimensions accounted for 81 of 92 exams in which three imaging tools all failed. Clinicians may not see these failures unless someone checks inputs before go-live.

Mapping local data to model inputs was often incomplete. One multi-hospital study mapped 4 of 6 constructs, and a Finnish study found waist-hip ratio absent from structured records. An echocardiography model returned predictions for 578 of 1541 eligible studies (38%). In one ED study, live and completed-data outputs agreed in 97.2% of encounters, which suggests that the effect of mismatch varies by model.

One randomized deployment enrolled low-income and racial and ethnic minority patients. It found discrepancies in variable definitions and missing data during real-time scoring. In a regional HIE, only 415 of 536 facilities shared diagnoses, and 21% of those shared procedures. Input gaps may be larger where records are fragmented, but no study tested verification in those settings.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software asks manufacturers to supply instructions for ensuring that input data are compatible with the device. A commentary on the EU AI Act describes site-specific and interoperability testing by facilities. These documents divide responsibility between vendors and deployers. No supplied study evaluates whether following either approach reduces errors.

In one surgical-duration study, user-adjusted Epic settings produced a mean absolute error of 35.3 minutes. Vendor-recommended settings with standardized definitions produced 20.1 minutes. Trial coordinators in another deployment reported time-intensive manual abstraction. These results suggest that verification requires IT staff time and configuration governance, although no study has measured its cost.

In a UK community optometry study, the AI system could not process images from 48.5% of 396 participants. Patients whose inputs fail may receive no result or a delayed result, and they may not know that a human review is needed. The supplied studies do not report how patients were informed or routed when inputs failed.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares deployments with and without a structured input-compatibility check before go-live. Stepped rollouts across sites with differing EHR and imaging configurations could measure unprocessable input rates, silent performance loss, and staff time required for verification.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Among the hazard studies, one trial enrolled low-income and racial and ethnic minority patients, one audit covered older adults, and one benchmark included people with disability. Whether verification helps in settings with fragmented or sparse records remains unknown.
